summary: This note is an overview of muscle as one of the four basic animal tissue types, covering its contractile proteins (actin and myosin), its formation during embryonic development (myogenesis), and its three vertebrate types: skeletal, smooth, and cardiac. It describes how each type is structured, how it is activated (voluntarily or involuntarily), and how its fibers differ in fiber type, mitochondria, and myoglobin content. It also covers the embryonic origin of muscle from paraxial mesoderm and the basic contraction mechanism shared by all three types.
one_line: Overview of muscle tissue: its three types, structure, contraction mechanism, embryonic development, and fiber classifications.
key_facts: Muscle is one of the four basic types of animal tissue and gives skeletal muscles the ability to contract.
Muscle tissue contains contractile proteins actin and myosin, which interact to cause movement; troponin and tropomyosin are regulatory proteins.
In vertebrates there are three muscle types: skeletal (striated), smooth (non-striated), and cardiac muscle.
Skeletal muscle fibres range from three to eight micrometers in width and 18 to 200 micrometers in length.
An average adult man is 42% skeletal muscle by body mass, and an average adult woman is 36%.
Cardiac muscle is found only in the walls of the heart as myocardium and is controlled involuntarily by the autonomic nervous system.
Cardiac muscle cells connect at branching, irregular angles known as intercalated discs, unlike the regular parallel bundles of skeletal muscle.
Smooth muscle is non-striated and involuntary, found in organs such as the esophagus, stomach, intestines, bronchi, uterus, urethra, bladder, and blood vessels.
Type I slow-twitch muscle is dense with capillaries and rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, giving it a red color.
Type IIx (also known as type IId) is the fastest muscle type in humans but can sustain only short anaerobic bursts of activity.
Muscle tissue has a density of about 1.06 kg/liter, approximately 15% denser than fat tissue at 0.9196 kg/liter.
All muscles are derived from paraxial mesoderm, which divides into somites, each with a myotome that forms muscle.
In skeletal muscle, contraction is stimulated by electrical impulses from motor nerves and facilitated by acetylcholine.
The word muscle comes from Latin musculus, a diminutive of mus meaning mouse, because the flexed biceps resembles a mouse's back.

entities.name: Myogenesis
entities.role: the process by which muscle is formed during embryonic development

entities.name: Actin
entities.role: contractile protein that interacts with myosin to cause movement

entities.name: Myosin
entities.role: contractile protein that interacts with actin to cause movement

entities.name: Skeletal muscle
entities.role: voluntary striated muscle anchored by tendons to bones, used for movement and posture

entities.name: Smooth muscle
entities.role: involuntary non-striated muscle found in walls of organs and blood vessels

entities.name: Cardiac muscle
entities.role: involuntary striated muscle found only in the myocardium of the heart

entities.name: Myocardium
entities.role: muscle tissue of the heart forming a thick middle layer between epicardium and endocardium

entities.name: Paraxial mesoderm
entities.role: embryonic tissue from which all muscles are derived

entities.name: Somite
entities.role: body segment of the paraxial mesoderm with sclerotome, dermatome, and myotome divisions

entities.name: Acetylcholine
entities.role: neurotransmitter that facilitates skeletal and many smooth muscle contractions

entities.name: Coronary arteries
entities.role: arteries that supply cardiac muscle with blood, oxygen and nutrients

entities.name: Sliding filament theory
entities.role: theory describing muscle contraction through movement of actin against myosin
